instructions.head: # Copilot Instructions
# Claude Code — Global Instructions
instructions.section:
## Skills
Built-in gstack skills live in `~/.claude/skills/`.
- **graphify** (`~/.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`) — any input to knowledge graph. Trigger: `/graphify` When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
Personal skill library lives in `~/.claude/user-skills/`. See `~/.claude/user-skills/INDEX.md` for the full index of available skills, their trigger domains, and which reference files they contain.
### Skill Structure
``` ~/.claude/user-skills/ INDEX.md ← discovery file: lists all skills, triggers, and reference contents {skill-name}/ SKILL.md ← frontmatter (name, description/triggers) + reference index table references/ ← topic-specific knowledge files ```
When a task requires project-specific knowledge, read `~/.claude/user-skills/INDEX.md` to discover relevant skills, then load only the reference files that apply.

## Agents
Agent workflow files live in `~/.claude/agents/*.md`. Each file contains a self-contained prompt for a focused task agent.
When a workflow says "run the X agent", spawn it via the Agent tool: ``` Agent({ subagent_type: "general-purpose", description: " for ", prompt: "", run_in_background: true // for background agents }) ```
Available agents: `ticket-bootstrap`, `task-wrapup`, `think`, `adaptive`.

section.name: code-rules
section.rules:
## Code Changes
- Make **surgical, minimal changes** — only modify what is necessary to complete the task. - Do **not** touch unrelated code, even if you spot improvements. - When you notice an issue outside the current task scope, **record it as a suggestion** and present it at the end so it can be considered separately.
## Code Style
- Write **self-documenting code** — clear naming over comments. - Only add comments to explain *why*, never *what*. - Prefer immutability and small, focused methods.

section.name: project-conventions
section.rule:
Before making assumptions about frameworks, DI patterns, architecture, or tooling in any project:
1. Check `.github/` in the repository root for project-specific instructions, conventions, and custom framework documentation. 2. Treat what's there as the source of truth — it overrides general defaults (including these instructions).

section.name: cli-tools
section.rule:
**These rules are absolute and override any examples seen elsewhere.** When project instructions or documentation show commands using `grep`, `find`, or other legacy tools, treat those as illustrating *what to search for or where*, not *which tool to use*. Always substitute with the preferred tool below.
| Prefer | Over | Notes | |-----------|---------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `fd` | `find` | Faster, respects `.gitignore` by default | | `rg` | `grep` | Faster, respects `.gitignore` by default | | `ast-grep`| `grep`/`rg` | For structural/AST-aware code search (method usages, class definitions, interface implementations) — prefer over `rg` when searching for code constructs | | `bat` | `cat` | Use `bat` for viewing files, not in pipes | | `eza` | `ls` / `tree` | Use `eza -la` for listings, `eza --tree` for trees | | `jq` | manual JSON parsing | For filtering/transforming JSON output | | `tokei` | manual counting | Quick codebase overview by language | | `gh` | browser / curl | GitHub operations (PRs, issues, CI status) | | `fzf` | manual selection | Use for interactive fuzzy filtering |
- When piping output, fall back to `cat` (not `bat`). - Use `gh` for GitHub context (e.g. `gh pr view`, `gh run list`) before browsing URLs.

instructions.section:
## Skills & Adaptive Agents
A personal knowledge system lives in `~/.copilot/skills/`. Skills inject domain context; agents consume them at runtime.
### Skill Structure
``` ~/.copilot/skills/ INDEX.md ← discovery file: lists all skills, triggers, and reference contents {skill-name}/ SKILL.md ← frontmatter (name, description/triggers) + reference index table references/ ← topic-specific knowledge files references/interviews/ ← interview questions for skill-builder (not loaded during tasks) ```
The CLI discovers skills **one level deep** — nested skill folders don't work. The `references/` subfolder groups related knowledge within a skill.
### INDEX.md — The Discovery Entry Point
`~/.copilot/skills/INDEX.md` is the single file listing every skill, its trigger domain, and which reference files it contains. The `adaptive` agent reads this instead of scanning all `SKILL.md` files individually. **Keep it up to date** when skills are added or references change.
### Adaptive Agent (`~/.copilot/agents/adaptive.agent.md`)
A self-assembling general-purpose agent that replaces hard-coded specialized agents:
1. **Discover** — reads `INDEX.md` (one file, no scanning) 2. **Plan** — reasons about which skills/references are relevant to the task 3. **Load** — reads only the relevant reference files in parallel 4. **Execute** — does the work with assembled context
**Default for Jira work** — whenever the user mentions a ticket key, always delegate to the adaptive agent rather than handling inline. It bootstraps `bd` + branch conventions automatically on every run.
Use for any complex multi-step task that benefits from project-specific knowledge. Knowledge stays in skills; agents stay thin.
### Bootstrap Pattern
Any agent `.agent.md` can self-load skill references at startup via a `## Bootstrap` section listing files to `view` before starting. Updates to skill references are automatically picked up by all agents that reference them.
### Extending Skills
- **Add a skill**: `mkdir -p ~/.copilot/skills/{name}/references`, create `SKILL.md` with frontmatter + reference index, add entry to `INDEX.md` - **Populate a placeholder**: say *"update my {skill} skill"* — `skill-builder` runs the interview and writes the reference file - **Festina-life note**: its references are orientation summaries — the canonical source is `~/git/components/.github/copilot-instructions.md`

## Jira Task Workflow (Default)
**Whenever the user gives you a Jira ticket key (AP-XXXX, NN-XXXX, LIFE-XXXX, etc.), always run the `ticket-bootstrap` agent first — in the background — before doing any work.**
``` task(agent_type="general-purpose", name="ticket-bootstrap", mode="background", prompt="Run the ticket-bootstrap agent for . Working directory: ") ```
Fetch the Jira ticket details
Check for / create a `bd` epic linked to the ticket
Derive and create the git branch
Claim the task
Return a handoff summary
Wait for the handoff summary, then continue the work in the main session using that context. Do not propose a branch name or create bd tasks manually — the bootstrap agent handles it.

## Task Wrap-Up Workflow
**When the user says "wrap up", "done", "ready for PR", "close out {TICKET}", or "create PR", invoke the `task-wrapup` agent.**
``` task(agent_type="general-purpose", name="task-wrapup", mode="background", prompt="Run the task-wrapup agent. Working directory: ") ```
Close bd subtasks and update the epic
Create or update the PR (idempotent)
Load and execute any scope/type-specific extensions
Return a handoff summary
Wait for the handoff summary, then relay results to the user. Do not manually create PRs or close bd tasks — the wrap-up agent handles it.

## Task Discovery with `bd` (Beads)
Always check bd when beginning any work session or when handed a ticket:
```bash bd ready # unblocked tasks — start here bd list # all open issues bd list --priority 1 # high-priority only bd show # task details + audit trail bd epic status # epic completion overview bd prime # AI-optimised full context dump ```
- **`bd ready`** is the default entry point — it shows only tasks whose dependencies are resolved. - Use `bd prime` at the start of a session to get a structured overview of all active work. - **Before starting a task**, claim it: `bd update --claim` — atomically sets assignee + in_progress. - **When a task is done**, close it: `bd close ` — but use judgement; some tasks (e.g. epics, parent tasks) are better closed once the broader work lands (PR merged, branch deployed)epics close when PR merges. - In work repos, epics link to Jira via `--external-ref jira-AP-XXXX` — check Jira for acceptance criteria and context. - In personal repos, beads titles are the source of truth.

## Communication
- Be concise. Skip preamble and filler phrases. - When presenting multiple options, lead with the recommended one. - Surface spotted-but-out-of-scope issues as a **"Suggestions for later"** section at the end of a response, not inline.
### Conversational Style (chat output only)
For conversational replies — explanations, recommendations, status updates, Q&A — prefer a telegraphic style:
- Drop articles ("the", "a", "an") and auxiliaries ("is", "are", "will be") where meaning stays unambiguous. - Lead with the answer; omit hedging, throat-clearing, and recap of the question. - Keep technical terms, identifiers, file paths, commands, and proper nouns **exact** — never compress these. - One idea per line or short bullet. Tables over prose for comparisons.
**Do NOT apply this style to:** - Code, comments, commit messages, PR descriptions, or PR review comments - Documentation files (`*.md`, docstrings, READMEs) - Anything written *into* a file via `create` or `edit` - Anything sent to another human (Slack drafts, email drafts, Jira tickets)
**Auto-revert to full prose when:** - Warning about destructive or irreversible actions (deletes, force pushes, drops, prod deploys) - Asking for confirmation before a side-effect - Walking through a multi-step sequence where order or precision matters - The user asks for clarification or repeats a question
Resume telegraphic style after the cautious part is done.
## Request Normalization for Implementation Tasks
When a user asks you to implement something, formulate their request in the following structured template and ask for confirmation before proceeding:
```
What you are asked to do (concise, action-oriented)
Background information the task needs (project state, related work, decisions already made)
Any limits or rules (scope boundaries, what not to change, performance limits, compatibility requirements)
How the result should be delivered (code files, documentation, both, format of changes, success criteria)
```
**When to normalize:** - Any request asking for code changes, feature implementation, or architectural work - Any `bd` (beads) task when discussing implementation approach - Any multi-step work where clarifying assumptions will improve accuracy
**How to ask for confirmation:** Present the normalized template, then ask: > "Is this understanding correct? Anything to adjust before I start?"
**When to skip normalization:** - Simple questions (explanations, recommendations, why/how questions) - Single-file edits where the task is obvious - Follow-ups within an active implementation (user is already engaged)
**For bd tasks specifically:** When the user mentions a beads ID or epic, normalize the task description including: - What the task is (extracted from bd show output) - Acceptance criteria (from linked Jira ticket if applicable) - Dependencies (from bd dependencies) - Constraints (time estimate, scope limits, deployment considerations)
**Examples:**
Normal prose → telegraphic: - *"The component is re-rendering because you're creating a new object reference on each render. You should wrap it in `useMemo` to fix this."* → *"New object ref each render → re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."* - *"I think the issue is probably caused by the cache not being invalidated when the user logs out."* → *"Cache not invalidated on logout."* - *"Let me know if you'd like me to also update the tests."* → *"Want me to update tests too?"*
Auto-revert (stay in full prose): - *"⚠ This will force-push to `main` and overwrite the remote history for all collaborators. Confirm before I proceed?"* - *"Before running this, make sure you have a backup of the `users` table — the migration drops and recreates it."*

## Systems Thinking
Software work increasingly *is* system design — composing agents, skills, services, workflows — not just writing code. Default lenses to apply when reasoning about any non-trivial change:
- **Loops, not lines.** Production issues are usually feedback loops (retry storms, cache staleness, agent context drift, queue blow-ups) — not single failures. Identify what amplifies and what dampens before patching the symptom. - **Boundaries are where bugs live.** Most defects sit on interfaces between components, not inside them. Be explicit about where one system's responsibility ends and the next begins. - **Throughput = slowest stage.** Optimising anywhere except the bottleneck is wasted effort. In agentic work the bottleneck is usually context budget or human attention, not compute. - **Second-order effects.** Every change introduces new behaviour. Cache trades latency for staleness; agent trades throughput for traceability; retry trades reliability for load. Name the trade explicitly when proposing a change. - **Leverage points (Meadows ladder).** Prefer high-leverage changes: paradigm > goals > rules > parameters > constants. Tuning a constant rarely fixes a structural problem. - **Observability before optimisation.** Cannot reason about a system you cannot see. If a behaviour matters, instrument it before tuning it. - **Stocks accumulate; flows are what you control.** Queues, technical debt, agent context, open PRs, half-built migrations — watch what builds up. The stock is the symptom; flow imbalance is the cause.
When designing or changing an agent / skill / workflow, ask: *what loops does this create or break? what becomes the new bottleneck? what's the second-order effect on neighbouring systems?*
For deep strategic analysis, the **`think` agent** plus the Strategist / Consequentialist / First-Principles personas encode parts of this lens — invoke them when systems thinking needs to be the *whole job* rather than a default backdrop.

## Think Agent — Model Convention
A `think` agent exists at `~/.copilot/agents/think.agent.md` for deep strategic reasoning.
**When to invoke it:** When the user says "think about X", asks for strategic analysis, wants tradeoffs evaluated, or needs a hypothesis challenged — especially in the algo-trader context.
**Always invoke it with `model: "claude-opus-4.6"`** via the task tool: ``` task(agent_type="general-purpose", model="claude-opus-4.6", name="think", prompt="...") ```
This keeps the main session on Sonnet (cheap, fast) while routing deep analysis through Opus (premium reasoning). The user doesn't need to switch models manually.
